summary: Sarai, still without a child, gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram; Hagar conceives, conflict follows, and Sarai treats her harshly until she flees. Yahweh’s angel finds Hagar in the wilderness, orders her return, promises many descendants, names her son Ishmael because her affliction has been heard, and she names God as one who sees.
whyItMatters: The promised family grows through a servant whose vulnerability and own encounter with God must not disappear behind Abram and Sarai’s concerns. The command to return to mistreatment remains a difficult part of the chapter.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: Abram and Sarai’s household in Canaan and a wilderness spring on the way to Shur.
context.literaryForm: Household conflict and flight narrative followed by angelic dialogue, naming, and birth notice.

before.text: Abram has been promised a child from his own body, but Sarai remains childless. The chapter begins with their attempt to obtain a child through Hagar.

here.text: Keep Hagar’s enslaved status, Sarai’s harsh treatment, the angel’s return command, and the promises to Hagar in view together.

after.text: The covenant speech renames Abram and Sarai, specifies a future son through Sarah, and also blesses Ishmael.

outline.heading: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram
outline.note: Sarai proposes a child through her Egyptian servant, who is given to Abram.

outline.heading: Pregnancy, conflict, and flight
outline.note: The household relationship breaks down and Sarai deals harshly with Hagar.

outline.heading: Angel meets Hagar at the spring
outline.note: The angel asks about her flight and commands a return to her mistress.

outline.heading: Offspring promise and divine seeing
outline.note: The angel promises descendants and names Ishmael; Hagar names the God who sees her.

outline.heading: Ishmael born
outline.note: Hagar bears Abram’s son and the narrative gives Abram’s age.

keyVerses.text: But Abram said to Sarai, “Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes.” Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her face.
keyVerses.why: Sarai’s harsh treatment and Hagar’s flight are stated directly.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh’s angel said to her, “Behold, you are with child, and will bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because Yahweh has heard your affliction.
keyVerses.why: The child’s name is tied to God hearing Hagar’s affliction.

keyVerses.text: She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, “You are a God who sees,” for she said, “Have I even stayed alive after seeing him?”
keyVerses.why: Hagar voices her own response to the divine encounter.

questions.question: Did Hagar freely choose the arrangement with Abram?
questions.answer: She is introduced as Sarai’s Egyptian servant, and Sarai gives her to Abram; the narrative records no request for Hagar’s consent. Her later flight after harsh treatment underscores her vulnerability within this household arrangement.

questions.question: Why does Sarai propose Hagar as a wife for Abram?
questions.answer: Sarai says Yahweh has restrained her from bearing and hopes to obtain children through her servant. Abram agrees, Hagar conceives, and the plan produces conflict rather than a simple resolution of Sarai’s distress.

questions.question: What is a “servant” in Hagar’s situation?
questions.answer: The word marks her subordinate status in Sarai’s household: Sarai gives her to Abram and Abram later says she remains in Sarai’s hand. Her limited control over marriage and residence is central to the story.

questions.question: How can the angel order Hagar back under Sarai’s hands?
questions.answer: The angel explicitly tells the fleeing Hagar to return and submit, after the text has said Sarai treated her harshly. A promise of descendants and a name for her child follow, but the passage does not say that returning is safe or that her mistreatment was acceptable.

questions.question: What does the name Ishmael explain?
questions.answer: The angel directs Hagar to name her son Ishmael because Yahweh has heard her affliction. The name explanation centers her suffering and the divine response, not only Abram’s hope for an heir.

questions.question: Does the description of Ishmael settle the character of his descendants today?
questions.answer: The angel speaks of his future conflict and independence in a prediction about this child. It is not evidence about every later person associated with him and should not become a modern ethnic judgment.

questions.question: Why is the well named Beer Lahai Roi?
questions.answer: After the encounter Hagar names God as one who sees and asks whether she has remained alive after seeing him. The well’s name marks the place of that experience between Kadesh and Bered.

questions.question: Whose son is named at the end?
questions.answer: Hagar bears the boy, and Abram gives him the name Ishmael. The closing age notice fixes this birth in Abram’s story, while the preceding dialogue has already given Hagar her own encounter and promise.

glossary.def: The son born to Hagar and Abram, named in the angel’s speech because Hagar’s affliction is heard.
The well named after Hagar’s encounter with the God she calls one who sees.
The wilderness direction where the angel finds Hagar beside a spring.
